title: Fortifying the Ocular Fortress: A Comprehensive Guide to Endophthalmitis Prevention
summary: Endophthalmitis, a devastating intraocular infection, remains a feared complication in ophthalmology. This comprehensive guide outlines evidence-based strategies across pre-operative, intra-operative, and post-operative phases to minimize its incidence and safeguard patient vision.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: Endophthalmitis is a severe intraocular inflammation of the vitreous cavity and/or aqueous humor, usually caused by microbial infection. It is a rare but devastating complication, primarily occurring after intraocular surgery (e.g., cataract extraction, intravitreal injection) or penetrating ocular trauma, leading to significant vision loss or even globe atrophy if not promptly and effectively managed. Prevention is paramount due to its severe prognosis.

sections.title: 2.1 Epidemiological Notes
content: Incidence varies by procedure: ~0.05-0.1% for cataract surgery (lower with intracameral antibiotics), 0.01-0.05% for intravitreal injections, up to 0.2% for glaucoma filtration surgery.
Post-traumatic endophthalmitis carries the highest incidence (4-30%), especially with retained intraocular foreign bodies.
Higher incidence reported in developing countries due to varied surgical standards and limited resources.

sections.title: 4. Pillars of Prevention: The Multi-Modal Approach
5. Pre-Operative Strategies
content: Patient Education: Emphasize hygiene, avoiding eye rubbing, and recognizing warning signs.
Risk Factor Identification: Control diabetes, manage blepharitis (topical azithromycin, tea tree oil, lid scrubs), dry eye, lacrimal system issues (dacryocystitis).

Topical Antibiotics: Pre-treatment with broad-spectrum topical antibiotics (e.g., moxifloxacin 0.5%, gatifloxacin 0.5%) 2-3 days prior to surgery, 4x/day. Evidence for routine use is debated but often practiced.
Povidone-Iodine (PVI) Prep: Essential. 5% PVI to periocular skin and eyelashes; 10% PVI diluted to 0.5-1% for conjunctival cul-de-sac. Apply 3-5 minutes before incision, then rinse.

sections.title: 6. Intra-Operative Asepsis & Technique: The Surgical Shield
content: Step 1: Strict Aseptic Technique — Proper hand scrubbing (alcohol-based rubs or iodophor/chlorhexidine scrub), sterile gowning, gloving, draping.
Step 2: Periocular Antisepsis — Application of 5-10% Povidone-Iodine to periocular skin, extending to forehead and malar regions. Allow to dry.
Step 3: Conjunctival Sac Antisepsis — Irrigation of conjunctival sac with 0.5-1% Povidone-Iodine solution for at least 30-60 seconds, then partially rinse.
Step 4: Eyelid Speculum & Draping — Use a sterile speculum to isolate lashes from the surgical field. Apply sterile drape with a sticky aperture to minimize contamination.
Step 5: Incision Construction — Create a self-sealing clear corneal incision or scleral tunnel incision to prevent external microbial ingress. Avoid excessive manipulation.
Step 6: Minimize Contact — Avoid instruments contacting lid margins or lashes. Use single-use instruments where possible.
Step 7: Intracameral Antibiotics — Inject at the conclusion of surgery. This is the SINGLE MOST EFFECTIVE intervention for preventing post-cataract endophthalmitis.

sections.title: 8. Post-Operative Care & Vigilance
content: Topical Antibiotics: Continue for 1-2 weeks post-surgery (e.g., moxifloxacin, gatifloxacin). Reduces bacterial load on ocular surface during wound healing. (Debate exists, but commonly practiced).
Topical Steroids: Control inflammation (e.g., prednisolone acetate 1%, difluprednate 0.05%, dexamethasone 0.1%). Reduces inflammatory response but does not protect against infection.
Wound Integrity Check: Ensure adequate wound hydration and self-sealing. Consider suture if wound leak detected.
Patient Education: Reinforce instructions on medication use, hand hygiene, avoiding eye rubbing, and immediate reporting of any 'red flag' symptoms (pain, vision loss, redness).

branches: - Systemic: Diabetes Mellitus, Immunosuppression (HIV, chemotherapy), Atopy/Psoriasis, Systemic infections (septicemia)
- Ocular: Blepharitis, Meibomian Gland Dysfunction, Conjunctivitis, Chronic Dacryocystitis, Pterygium, Prior Ocular Surgery, Compromised Corneal Surface
- Behavior: Poor Hygiene, Non-compliance with medications
- Incision Type: Clear corneal (compared to scleral tunnel), non-self-sealing wounds, wound dehiscence
- Surgical Complexity: Prolonged surgery, Posterior capsular rupture, Vitreous loss, use of multiple instruments
- IOL Type/Position: Atypical IOLs (e.g., sulcus-fixated), Suture fixation
- Surgical Environment: Breach in sterile technique, contaminated solutions/instruments
- Post-operative topical steroid overuse (unlikely if antibiotics used)

sections.title: 10. Red Flags / Emergency Signs Post-Surgery
content: Progressive DECREASE IN VISION (out of proportion to expected post-op course)
SEVERE OCULAR PAIN (disproportionate to typical post-op discomfort), often worsening over time
Marked REDNESS of the eye (circumcorneal injection, chemosis)
Hypopyon (pus level in the anterior chamber)
Lid edema and periorbital swelling
Corneal edema and infiltrates (less common but severe)
Vitreous haze or white exudates (on slit-lamp or fundoscopy)
Loss of red reflex or poor view of fundus
IOL deposits or inflammatory membranes on IOL/capsule

sections.title: 13. Key Clinical Pearls for Prevention
content: Povidone-iodine is the single most important and cost-effective antiseptic measure. Do not skip it!
Intracameral antibiotics (Cefuroxime 1mg or Moxifloxacin 100-200µg) are the strongest evidence-based prophylactic measure for post-cataract endophthalmitis.
Meticulous wound construction and hydration are critical for preventing external bacterial ingress.
Aggressively treat pre-existing blepharitis or dry eye before elective intraocular surgery.
Prompt recognition and referral of 'red flag' symptoms can differentiate endophthalmitis from sterile inflammation and save vision.

sections.title: 14. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: ESCRS Endophthalmitis Study (2007): Landmark randomized clinical trial demonstrating 5-fold reduction in endophthalmitis with intracameral cefuroxime (1mg in 0.1ml) at the conclusion of cataract surgery. No significant benefit from pre-operative topical levofloxacin.
AAO Preferred Practice Patterns: Strongly recommend perioperative Povidone-Iodine application and consider intracameral antibiotics for cataract surgery.

Moxifloxacin vs. Cefuroxime: Growing adoption of intracameral moxifloxacin (100-200µg) due to its broad spectrum, ready-to-use formulation (from preservative-free topical drops), and excellent intraocular penetration, despite lacking a large-scale RCT like the ESCRS study.

HORV and Vancomycin: The association of hemorrhagic occlusive retinal vasculitis (HORV) with intracameral vancomycin (especially in bilateral simultaneous surgery) has led to recommendations against its routine use.

Role of Post-Op Topical Antibiotics: Current evidence suggests minimal additional benefit of post-operative topical antibiotics when intracameral antibiotics are used, but practice patterns vary. Some studies indicate they may prolong resistance development.

sections.title: 15. Special Population Considerations
content: Diabetic Patients: Higher risk of endophthalmitis. Emphasize stringent glycemic control pre-operatively and meticulous attention to all prophylactic measures.

Immunocompromised Patients (HIV, transplant, systemic chemotherapy): Increased risk, often with atypical organisms (fungal, less common bacteria). May warrant broader-spectrum or longer duration antibiotic prophylaxis, and lower threshold for aggressive management.

Pediatric Patients: Often undergo surgery under general anesthesia, which may mask early symptoms. Compliance with post-op medications can be challenging. Higher incidence of post-traumatic endophthalmitis.
Patients with Blepharitis/MGD: Requires aggressive pre-operative treatment (e.g., topical azithromycin, hypochlorous acid, lid scrubs) to reduce bacterial load on lid margin and lashes.

sections.title: 16. Surgical Management of a Suspected Case (Briefly, for Context)
content: Step 1: Immediate Referral to Retina/Endophthalmitis Specialist.
Step 2: Aqueous/Vitreous Tap for Microscopy (Gram stain, KOH) & Culture (aerobic, anaerobic, fungal).
Step 3: Intravitreal Antibiotics Injection (e.g., Vancomycin 1mg/0.1mL + Ceftazidime 2.25mg/0.1mL or Amikacin 0.4mg/0.1mL).
Step 4: Consider Vitrectomy if severe vision loss (hand motion or worse), non-responsive to injections, or fungal etiology suspected (EVRS study criteria).
Step 5: Topical and Systemic Antibiotics (adjunctive).

sections.title: 17. Future Directions in Prevention
sections.content: Research continues into novel preventative strategies, including sustained-release antibiotic implants, antimicrobial coatings for intraocular lenses, and advanced diagnostic techniques for rapid pathogen identification to guide targeted prophylaxis. The goal is to further reduce the already low, but still significant, incidence of this vision-threatening condition.
